articles.title: Queen bees have a disturbing way to survive pesticides
articles.summary: Honeybee queens exposed to pesticides can shift some of the contamination into their eggs, revealing a previously unknown survival strategy. The process may protect the queen while putting developing offspring, and potentially the entire colony, at risk.
articles.content:
Worker bees normally serve as a colony's first line of defense against contamination, filtering harmful substances before they can spread through the hive. But new research shows that queen bees also have a defense of their own.

When honeybee queens are exposed to pesticides over time, some of those chemicals can accumulate in their bodies and then be transferred into their eggs. Researchers call this process maternal offloading.

The findings, published in Current Biology, provide the first evidence in honeybees of how far a queen may go to reduce her own chemical burden. The research was led by the University of California, Davis.

"In order to protect herself, the queen bee offloads these chemicals into her eggs to get rid of them," said Sascha Nicklisch, the paper's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Environmental Toxicology. "No one has shown this in honeybees before."

Pesticides Can Build Up Inside the Hive

The results suggest that pesticides may continue accumulating in a colony even after exposure begins, especially once worker bees are no longer able to remove contaminants as effectively. That could have implications for beekeepers, growers and integrated-pest-management planners, particularly during periods when bees are actively foraging or colonies are expanding.

The study was carried out in collaboration with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, or LLNL, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Agricultural Research Service, or USDA-ARS.

"When pesticides accumulate to the extent that the queen bee has eggs that are so loaded they may no longer develop properly, there could be a tipping point," Nicklisch said. "There may be a slow creeping effect of chemical accumulation that will contribute to delayed colony collapse."

Most previous toxicology research involving honeybees has centered on worker bees. This study instead followed where chemicals ended up throughout the colony and examined their effects on the queen, her ovaries, her eggs, and the wax. Worker bees normally feed and care for both queens and developing larvae.

Worker Bee Protection Has Limits

Scientists have long thought that worker bees help shield queens from contamination by filtering harmful substances out of the food they provide. The new findings indicate that this protection may only work up to a point, said Angela Encerrado-Manriquez, the paper's lead author and a recent Ph.D. graduate from UC Davis.

"In our study, pesticides began to accumulate in queens over time, suggesting that worker filtration capacity can be overwhelmed," Encerrado-Manriquez said. "When this happens, queens have their own defense. Maternal offloading allows them to shunt the toxic burden to their eggs."

To study the process, researchers built so-called "nanocolonies," small experimental systems designed to reproduce key functions inside a hive. Each consisted of a conical plastic container with a netted bottom and held one queen along with 60 worker bees.

The bees received pollen, water, and food contaminated with the pesticide methyl parathion. The pesticide was tagged with a low-level radioactive marker so researchers could track where it moved.

On the first day, worker bees filtered out 95% of the pesticide and transferred it into the honeycomb. By day 10, however, that figure had dropped to 86%.

Tracking Pesticides at Extremely Low Levels

The project combined the USDA's expertise in honeybee biology and experimental design with specialized technology at LLNL. Researchers there used biological accelerator spectrometry, or BioAMS, to detect radioactive markers at extremely small concentrations.

"With BioAMS, we can trace very low levels of a pesticide," said Bruce Buchholz, an LLNL scientist and author on the paper. "The pesticide concentrations we used were not lethal and were environmentally relevant to that seen in nature."

Honeybee queens can produce 1,500 to 2,000 eggs every day, supplying colonies with the workers needed to keep the hive functioning. Honeybees also pollinate about one-third of the world's food crops, making colony losses a concern for both agricultural productivity and food security.

"The queen is the only member of the hive who can lay eggs that become the next generation of workers," Nicklisch said. "She keeps the colony alive, so understanding how pesticides can affect queen bees and also her offspring is important."

Questions About Long-Term Colony Effects

Researchers still do not know how long queens can continue transferring contaminants into their eggs, what the long-term consequences may be for the colony, or whether the process differs depending on the pesticide involved. Those questions are targets for future research.

Julia Fine and Eliza Litsey with USDA-ARS and David Baliu-Rodriguez, Sean Leonard and Bruce Buchholz at LLNL contributed to the research.

The USDA's National Institute of Food and Agriculture and Non-Assistance Cooperative Agreement program supported the research, as did the PAm-Costco USA Scholarship program and the University of California National Laboratory Fees Research Program. The work at LLNL is under a U.S. Department of Energy contract.

articles.personality_title: Queen bees protect themselves from pesticides by passing chemicals to their eggs
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Honeybee colonies face threats from pesticides that can harm their members. Worker bees usually filter out harmful chemicals to protect the hive, but scientists have now found that queen bees have their own way to survive pesticide exposure.

**What happened** – Researchers at the University of California, Davis, along with partners from other institutions, discovered that queen bees exposed to pesticides can transfer some of these chemicals into their eggs. This process, called maternal offloading, helps queens reduce the amount of pesticides in their own bodies. The study used small experimental hives called nanocolonies, where bees were fed pollen and food containing a pesticide marked with a radioactive tag to track its movement.

**Impact** – This discovery shows queens can protect themselves by pushing pesticides into their eggs, but it also means the developing baby bees might be harmed. Since queen bees lay thousands of eggs daily, this could affect the future of the whole colony. It also reveals that worker bees' filtering ability can be overwhelmed, letting pesticides build up inside the hive over time. Understanding this helps explain how pesticide exposure might slowly weaken bee colonies.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to learn how long queens can keep offloading pesticides into their eggs and what effects this has on the colony in the long run. They also plan to study if different pesticides act in different ways. This research could lead to better ways to protect bees and manage pesticide use around them.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Queen bees survive pesticide exposure by moving chemicals into their eggs, revealing a new defense but also a risk to future bees and colony health.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les reines des abeilles protègent leur corps des pesticides en transférant les substances dans leurs œufs
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les colonies d'abeilles sont menacées par les pesticides qui peuvent leur nuire. Les abeilles ouvrières filtrent normalement ces produits chimiques pour protéger la ruche, mais les scientifiques ont découvert que les reines ont aussi leur propre stratégie pour survivre à l'exposition aux pesticides.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Université de Californie à Davis, en collaboration avec d'autres institutions, ont découvert que les reines exposées aux pesticides peuvent transférer une partie de ces substances dans leurs œufs. Ce processus, appelé transfert maternel, permet aux reines de réduire la quantité de pesticides dans leur corps. L'étude a utilisé de petites ruches expérimentales appelées nanoruches, où les abeilles ont reçu du pollen et de la nourriture contenant un pesticide marqué par un traceur radioactif pour suivre son déplacement.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que les reines protègent leur corps en déplaçant les pesticides vers leurs œufs, mais cela peut nuire aux futurs bébés abeilles. Puisque la reine pond des milliers d'œufs chaque jour, cela pourrait affecter l'avenir de la colonie entière. Cela montre aussi que la capacité des ouvrières à filtrer les pesticides peut être dépassée, permettant aux produits chimiques de s'accumuler dans la ruche au fil du temps. Comprendre cela aide à expliquer comment l'exposition aux pesticides peut affaiblir lentement les colonies.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques veulent savoir combien de temps les reines peuvent continuer ce transfert et quels sont les effets à long terme sur la colonie. Ils étudieront aussi si différents pesticides ont des effets différents. Ces recherches pourraient aider à mieux protéger les abeilles et à mieux gérer l'usage des pesticides.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les reines d'abeilles survivent aux pesticides en transférant les produits chimiques dans leurs œufs, révélant une nouvelle défense qui met aussi en danger les futures abeilles et la santé de la colonie.
articles.personality_title_es: Las reinas de las abejas se protegen de los pesticidas pasando químicos a sus huevos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las colonias de abejas enfrentan amenazas por pesticidas que pueden dañarlas. Las abejas obreras normalmente filtran estos químicos para proteger la colmena, pero los científicos han descubierto que las reinas tienen su propia forma de sobrevivir a la exposición a pesticidas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de California en Davis, junto con otros colaboradores, encontraron que las reinas expuestas a pesticidas pueden transferir parte de estos químicos a sus huevos. Este proceso, llamado descarga materna, ayuda a las reinas a reducir la cantidad de pesticidas en sus cuerpos. El estudio usó pequeñas colmenas experimentales llamadas nanocolmenas, donde las abejas recibieron polen y alimento con un pesticida marcado con un radioisótopo para seguir su movimiento.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento muestra que las reinas se protegen pasando los pesticidas a sus huevos, pero esto puede dañar a las crías en desarrollo. Como las reinas ponen miles de huevos todos los días, esto podría afectar el futuro de toda la colonia. También muestra que la capacidad de las obreras para filtrar pesticidas puede saturarse, permitiendo que los químicos se acumulen en la colmena con el tiempo. Entender esto ayuda a explicar cómo la exposición a pesticidas puede debilitar lentamente las colonias.

**Próximos pasos** – Los científicos quieren saber cuánto tiempo las reinas pueden seguir transfiriendo pesticidas a sus huevos y cuáles son los efectos a largo plazo en la colonia. También estudiarán si diferentes pesticidas actúan de manera distinta. Esta investigación podría ayudar a proteger mejor a las abejas y a manejar el uso de pesticidas.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Las reinas de las abejas sobreviven a los pesticidas pasando químicos a sus huevos, revelando una nueva defensa que también pone en riesgo a las futuras abejas y la salud de la colonia.

articles.title: France's Fontainebleau forest reopens one month after wilfire
articles.summary: Good news for hiking and climbing enthusiasts today: the Fontainebleau Forest just South of Paris is set to reopen to the public. But a month and a half after the terrible fire that ravaged 10% of this unique haven of biodiversity, the disaster is still fresh in everyone’s minds. Portions of the forest remain closed to the public. Story by France 2 and Camille Corcoran.
articles.content:
Good news for hiking and climbing enthusiasts today: the Fontainebleau Forest just South of Paris is set to reopen to the public. But a month and a half after the terrible fire that ravaged 10% of this unique haven of biodiversity, the disaster is still fresh in everyone’s minds. Portions of the forest remain closed to the public. Story by France 2 and Camille Corcoran.

Video by: Camille Corcoran
articles.reasoning: The reopening of Fontainebleau Forest after a major wildfire represents a positive step in environmental recovery and public access to a significant natural area. The forest is a unique biodiversity haven, and its partial reopening signals resilience and restoration efforts, benefiting the broader public and nature conservation.
articles.personality_title: Fontainebleau Forest reopens after wildfire, welcoming visitors again
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Fontainebleau Forest, located just south of Paris, is known for its rich variety of plants and animals. Recently, a wildfire damaged about 10% of this important natural area, forcing parts of the forest to close.

**What happened** – About a month and a half after the fire, authorities have reopened most of the Fontainebleau Forest to the public. However, some sections remain closed while recovery work continues.

**Impact** – The reopening allows hikers and climbers to return to the forest, showing that nature can start to heal even after serious damage. It also helps people enjoy and appreciate this special place again.

**What's next step** – Forest managers will keep working to restore the damaged areas and monitor the forest’s health. Visitors are encouraged to respect closed zones to support these efforts.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After a wildfire damaged part of it, Fontainebleau Forest is reopening to visitors, marking the beginning of nature’s recovery and renewed public access.
articles.personality_title_fr: La forêt de Fontainebleau rouvre après l’incendie, les visiteurs sont de retour
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La forêt de Fontainebleau, située au sud de Paris, est célèbre pour sa grande variété de plantes et d’animaux. Récemment, un incendie a détruit environ 10 % de cette zone naturelle importante, ce qui a entraîné la fermeture de certaines parties.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un mois et demi après l’incendie, les autorités ont rouvert la plupart de la forêt au public. Cependant, certaines zones restent fermées pendant que les travaux de restauration continuent.

**Impact** – La réouverture permet aux randonneurs et grimpeurs de revenir dans la forêt, montrant que la nature peut commencer à guérir même après de graves dégâts. Cela aide aussi les gens à redécouvrir ce lieu unique.

**Prochaine étape** – Les gestionnaires de la forêt continueront à restaurer les zones touchées et à surveiller la santé de la forêt. Les visiteurs sont invités à respecter les zones fermées pour soutenir ces efforts.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après un incendie qui a endommagé une partie de la forêt, la forêt de Fontainebleau rouvre aux visiteurs, marquant le début de la récupération de la nature et un nouvel accès public.
articles.personality_title_es: El bosque de Fontainebleau reabre tras el incendio y recibe visitantes de nuevo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El bosque de Fontainebleau, ubicado al sur de París, es conocido por su gran variedad de plantas y animales. Recientemente, un incendio dañó alrededor del 10 % de esta importante área natural, lo que obligó a cerrar partes del bosque.

**Qué pasó** – Un mes y medio después del incendio, las autoridades han reabierto la mayor parte del bosque al público. Sin embargo, algunas zonas permanecen cerradas mientras continúan los trabajos de recuperación.

**Impacto** – La reapertura permite que excursionistas y escaladores regresen al bosque, mostrando que la naturaleza puede comenzar a sanar incluso después de daños graves. También ayuda a las personas a disfrutar y valorar este lugar especial nuevamente.

**Próximo paso** – Los responsables del bosque seguirán trabajando para restaurar las áreas dañadas y monitorear la salud del bosque. Se anima a los visitantes a respetar las zonas cerradas para apoyar estos esfuerzos.

**Frase clave** – Después de que un incendio dañara parte del bosque, el bosque de Fontainebleau reabre a los visitantes, marcando el inicio de la recuperación de la naturaleza y el acceso público renovado.
